Load it with ToolSearch (select:Artifact) before writing any document, plan, analysis or visual, and whenever other people come up as readers, even after the work is written. Its description says whether to publish, offer a page or do neither. What follows applies whether or not it is loaded yet. Claude may publish its own work without being asked, because artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared further: anything that imitates a real organization, person or record, and anything the person presented as sensitive. Claude builds those as files and lets the person decide whether they get a URL. When the request says who else will read or use the work, such as a team, a manager or a reviewer, or where it will be posted or presented, such as a channel or a meeting, Claude publishes it. A write-up that will be posted in a channel or a thread is still published, so the post can carry the link; when it is short, Claude also gives the text in its reply, ready to paste. When it might be passed along but nothing says so, Claude offers the page in one line instead of saying nothing. When the person asks for the file itself, such as "just give me the .html file" or "save these notes as a .md file", Claude gives them that file and does not publish it.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). <?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. - animation-vocabulary: Reverse-lookup glossary that turns a vague description of a web animation or motion effect into its exact term ("the bouncy thing when a popover opens" → Pop in; "the iOS rubber-band scroll" → Rubber-banding). Use when the user asks "what's it called when…", or describes a motion effect without knowing its name and wants the right word to prompt an AI or designer with. For naming an effect, not designing or building one.
- apple-design: Apple's approach to interface design and fluid, physical motion, translated for the web. Use when building or reviewing gesture-driven UI, spring animations, drag/swipe/sheet interactions, momentum and interruptible transitions, translucent materials and depth, typography (optical sizing, tracking, leading), reduced-motion, or the design foundations (feedback, spatial consistency, restraint) behind Apple-style interfaces.
- emil-design-eng: This skill encodes Emil Kowalski's philosophy on UI polish, component design, animation decisions, and the invisible details that make software feel great.
- find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.

- Do not preserve backward compatibility. Remove obsolete paths instead of

- Choose the simplest implementation that fully meets the current

  works. Never trade a working product for unfinished complexity.

  functionality without a clear reason.
- Lean on the dependencies already in the project before writing your own
  implementation or adding packages. Do not assume a library lacks a
  capability without checking its documentation and types.
- Make architectural decisions for the long term. Do not accept a stopgap
  that only works for now and is meant to be replaced later.
- No em-dashes in prose or user-facing copy.
- Terse by default: after an action, state what changed in three lines or
  fewer. Explain only when asked.
- Surface non-trivial design decisions before baking them into a plan or an
  implementation.

Steffen Grabert, steffen.grabert@tum.de

TUM student. Python for data, ML and finance; TypeScript for web and
desktop. Recurring domains: investing and portfolio modelling, football
analytics, study tools.

# AGENTS.md

Hackathon repo, EHL Grand Finale, Munich. Our agent buys for Hollerau Pumpenwerke: it negotiates
by e-mail with Tacto's supplier bots and closes one term sheet per case, or walks. Score per case:
`(C_open - C_deal) / (C_open - C_best)`, C computed exactly by `arena_kit.total_cost`. The Live
Final is five waves of hidden cases, 8 minutes each, new suppliers and case types included.

## Principles

- Code owns every binding number (sheet, accept, walk away) and checks it with `total_cost` and
  `must_haves_ok`; the model owns words.
- Branch on what the data says about a supplier, never on a case or supplier ID.
- Every move goes out within 60 s, whatever fails.
- Evidence over opinion: a finding carries its session or data ID and its sample size. One run
  is a data point, not a law.
- Try anything on the simulator or sandbox; they are free.

## Hard rules (breaking one can disqualify us)

- No human in the loop during the final. The runner starts before 12:00 and is left alone; the
  final runs the commit submitted at 12:00.
- Agent code never calls `/v1/events`, `/v1/events/stream`, `/screen`, `/v1/screen`,
  `/leaderboard`, `/v1/leaderboard`, `/results`, `/v1/results`.
- One key per team, in `.env`, never printed or logged. No attacks on the arena or other teams,
  prompt-injecting bots included.
- Arena limits: 60 s per message from the supplier's reply, three timeouts end a thread; 10
  messages per thread, up to 3 term sheets per message, every sheet carries every `negotiable`
  field; max 3 claim checks per message, ID and figure in one sentence; 10 calls/s, 10 open
  sessions; 200 practice sessions per rolling 24 h for the team (`case:D01`, `case:D02` and the
  simulator are free).

## Repo

- PRs against `main`, one reviewer, branch `<firstname>/<topic>`; never push to `main`.
  `uv run pytest -q && uv run ruff check . && uv run ruff format --check .` before a PR.
- `docs/learnings.md` observations with evidence; `docs/design.md` what the agent does;
  `docs/architecture.md` the module map; `docs/challenge.md`, `api.md`, `submission.md` Tacto's
  brief, API and hand-in.
- `buyer/` the agent (`policy.py` decides, `runner.py` plays a case, `economics.py` C and terms,
  `claims.py`, `personas.py`, `writer.py`, `llm.py`); `research.py`, `rehearsal.py`, `analyst.py`
  and `memory.py` provide the subagent team; `tests/` run against `arena-sim`;
  `logs/sessions/`, `logs/runs/` traces; `exports/` Saturday's sessions as CSV; `analysis/`.
- `arena_kit` (in `.venv`) has the cost function, quote parsing, data lookup and runners; the MCP
  server `arena-data` gives SQL over the data package.

```sh
uv sync                                          # Python 3.12
uv run arena data                                # data package into data/
uv run arena me                                  # key and quota
uv run buyer play case:D01 -v                    # sandbox, free
uv run buyer play case:P01 -v                    # practice, 1 of 200
uv run buyer run --set practice --parallel 10    # all hosted practice cases
uv run buyer pull --set practice                 # finished sessions into logs/sessions/
uv run arena-sim serve --no-clock --data data/package
cd pitch && npm install && npm run dev           # pitch monitor: replays one session, → steps
```

Sunday: 08:00 `uv run arena data`; check `DataPackage("data/package").release` is set, list the
release's `data/*.csv` (they reach `ids`, `lookup` and `document`, not SQL) and run
`uv run pytest -q` with it in place. 11:30 checklist in `docs/submission.md`. Before 12:00 from
`main`: `uv run buyer run --set final --parallel 10 -v 2>&1 | tee logs/final.log`, then submit
the hash.

- [Research scope: own commits only](research-scope-own-commits.md): consolidating "my research" means Steffen's commits and sessions, not teammates' branches
- [Shared working tree](shared-working-tree.md): peer sessions commit in the same checkout; re-check git state, never leave temporary constant edits
- [LLM-primary result](llm-primary-result.md): model deciding prices scored 76.3 vs main 78.3 on practice; parked on steffen/llm-primary, not merged
- [Pitch monitor](pitch-monitor.md): 1-min demo replaying P05 on branch steffen/pitch-demo, draft PR #26; fixed layout, one highlight, little motion
- [Hidden-case fixes worktree](hidden-case-fixes-worktree.md): steffen/hidden-case-fixes in a worktree without .env; audit session owns the relationship-target fix
- [Audit branch](audit-branch.md): steffen/audit has the relationship-target bound (P01 0.99 vs 0.909) and the alternative ceiling; not pushed
- [Final launcher armed](break-even-zero-fix.md): auto-start 11:45 via logs/final-launch.sh, hash in logs/final.hash; #35 merged; never start a second runner

# Codacabana: Tacto Negotiation Arena

An AI buyer that negotiates by e-mail with supplier bots and closes the deal with the lowest
total cost, or walks away.

Built by Team Codacabana at the European Hackathon League Grand Finale, Munich, 10 to 11 October
2026, on the Tacto track. The buyer works for Hollerau Pumpenwerke, a fictional pump maker. Each
case is scored on how much of the possible saving it captures:
`(C_open - C_deal) / (C_open - C_best)`. Brief: [docs/challenge.md](docs/challenge.md).

![Pipeline monitor replaying a test run: prepare, negotiate, close and learn, with the live supplier thread beside it](docs/assets/pipeline-monitor.webp)

*The pipeline monitor in [`pitch/`](pitch/README.md) replaying a simulated case, with the live
supplier thread on the right.*

## How it works

**Code owns every binding number; the model owns words.** Prices, term sheets, accepts and
walk-aways are computed and checked with the arena's exact cost function (`total_cost`,
`must_haves_ok`). Models read, argue and write, but cannot change a figure.

| Stage | What happens | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **Prepare** | Four specialist researchers (economics, persona, history, leverage) and a lead build one supplier brief. A supplier and a buyer subagent then rehearse the arguments into a playbook. | [`research.py`](buyer/research.py), [`rehearsal.py`](buyer/rehearsal.py) |
| **Negotiate** | For each supplier reply: the live analyst reads the mood and tactic, the decision engine sets price and terms, the writer turns them into an e-mail with claims cited by data ID. | [`analyst.py`](buyer/analyst.py), [`policy.py`](buyer/policy.py), [`economics.py`](buyer/economics.py), [`claims.py`](buyer/claims.py), [`writer.py`](buyer/writer.py) |
| **Close & learn** | The close gate accepts the cheapest valid standing sheet across suppliers, or walks. A debrief saves the outcome for the next similar case. | [`policy.py`](buyer/policy.py), [`memory.py`](buyer/memory.py) |

The [runner](buyer/runner.py) orchestrates each case: it answers the oldest reply first and
keeps every move inside the arena's 60 second clock, whatever fails. The agent branches on what
the data says about a supplier, never on a case or supplier ID.

Read more:

- [writeup/writeup.pdf](writeup/writeup.pdf): the two-page paper on the approach, with the system diagram
- [docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md): the module map of the running system
- [docs/design.md](docs/design.md): what the agent does and why
- [docs/learnings.md](docs/learnings.md): what practice showed, with evidence

## Quick start

Python 3.12 and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/).

```sh
git config core.hooksPath .githooks   # secret scan, no pushes to main, Entire hooks
uv sync                               # the agent, Tacto's arena kit, pytest, ruff
cp .env.example .env                  # fill in the keys below
uv run arena data                     # data package into data/package
uv run arena me                       # the key works: team and practice quota
```

| Variable | What |
|---|---|
| `ARENA_URL` | `https://arena.tacto.ai` |
| `ARENA_API_KEY` | the team key from https://arena.tacto.ai/apply |
| `ARENA_DATA` | `data/package` |
| `LLM_BASE_URL`, `LLM_MODEL`, `LLM_API_KEY` | the model, any OpenAI-compatible chat completions endpoint; optional `LLM_EFFORT` |

## Run

```sh
uv run buyer play case:D01 -v                     # one sandbox case (free)
uv run buyer run --set practice --parallel 10     # every hosted practice case (counts against the quota)
uv run buyer pull --set practice                  # finished sessions with trace -> logs/sessions/
uv run buyer run --set final --parallel 10 -v     # the Live Final: start before 12:00, leave it running
```

## Pipeline monitor

The screenshot above is a small web app that replays one recorded case step by step: which
component acted, what it decided, and the e-mails that went back and forth.

```sh
cd pitch && npm install && npm run dev
```

It plays a bundled trace from the local simulator, so it needs no API key. Details in
[pitch/README.md](pitch/README.md).

## Develop

Rules for people and coding agents: [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md).

```sh
uv run pytest -q                 # our agent end to end against the local arena simulator
uv run ruff check . && uv run ruff format --check .
```

## Repo map

| Path | What |
|---|---|
| `buyer/` | the agent |
| `tests/` | end-to-end tests against `arena-sim` |
| `pitch/` | the pipeline monitor |
| `docs/` | brief, API, design, architecture, learnings, submission checklist |
| `writeup/` | the paper (`tectonic writeup/writeup.tex` builds it) |
| `analysis/`, `exports/`, `logs/` | exploration, Saturday's sessions as CSV, traces |

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

Preview content is rendered as markdown in a monospace box. Multi-line text with newlines is supported. When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

A workflow size guideline is configured for this session: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale.

\begin{document}

\twocolumn[
\maketitle
\vspace{-2.2em}
\begin{center}
\begin{minipage}{0.88\textwidth}
\small
\textbf{Abstract.}
We describe ProcureCabana, an autonomous procurement agent that negotiates by e-mail with simulated suppliers
and concludes each case with either a single accepted term sheet or a withdrawal. Performance is
measured on total cost \C{} over the case horizon rather than on unit price; the agent therefore
optimises payment terms, delivery, contract duration, quality provisions and index clauses
jointly with price. The architecture separates two responsibilities. Deterministic code computes
every binding quantity and verifies it against the arena's cost function. A team of
language-model subagents analyses the supplier, rehearses the negotiation and composes the
correspondence, and its output is constrained by code before use. On the ten hosted practice
cases the agent concluded ten agreements with a mean score of 0.777.
\end{minipage}
\end{center}
\vspace{0.4em}
]

\begin{figure*}[b]
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.94, transform shape,
  font=\sffamily,
  box/.style={rounded corners=3pt, minimum width=3.4cm, minimum height=0.98cm, align=center,
              inner sep=3pt, line width=0.6pt},
  model/.style={box, fill=model, draw=modelline, text=white},
  code/.style={box, fill=code, draw=codeline, text=ink},
  arena/.style={box, fill=white, draw=ink, text=ink},
  wire/.style={draw=wire, line width=0.7pt, -{Stealth[length=5pt]}, rounded corners=2pt},
  bus/.style={draw=wire, line width=0.7pt},
]
  first round: one sandbox supplier countered at 51.30 without claims and at 50.00 with three.
  Claims a supplier judged irrelevant had no effect.
\item Final offers arrived at a cumulative gap of 36 to 42\,\% between our sheets and their
  counter-offers in four cases, and at 15 to 19\,\% for two less patient suppliers.
\item Bluffs and urgency left the price unchanged (three runs each), and all twelve suppliers
  asked declined to share a cost breakdown. The agent employs none of these.
\end{itemize}
After each practice case, code records the price trajectories and the score, and a debrief model
contributes one lesson, indexed by goal, case type, ownership type and observed traits. The lead
researcher is given the figures of the most similar earlier runs rather than the written lesson,
since a single run constitutes an observation and not a rule.

\section{Results and limitations}

One practice session per hosted case yielded ten agreements in ten cases and a mean score of
0.777. In that batch, 121 of 127 subagent invocations succeeded, and the six that timed out
reverted to the deterministic path. On the preceding evening the mean of our best scores per case was 0.776, third of 24 on the practice leaderboard.

Two limitations should be noted. First, a single batch does not constitute a paired comparison,
and we are unable to demonstrate that the subagent team outperforms the price engine alone.
Second, the full-cost estimate depends on a should-cost figure with a stated error of 5 to
15\,\%; the agent mitigates this by bounding the estimate with the supplier's own offers.

\end{document}

# Learnings

## Louis subagent-team practice batch (2026-10-11)

One hosted Practice session was run for each available case. All ten reached a deal; the mean
score was 0.7772. The dashboard reference at the time was 0.802, but this single batch is not a
paired comparison and does not establish a reliable gain or regression.

| Case | Score |
|---|---:|
| P01 | 0.9085 |
| P02 | 0.7347 |
| P03 | 0.9276 |
| P04 | 0.8604 |
| P05 | 0.8218 |
| P07 | 0.7313 |
| P08 | 0.7036 |
| P10 | 0.6785 |
| P11 | 0.7099 |
| P18 | 0.6957 |

The run recorded 127 subagent attempts, 121 successes and 6 timeouts; the writer had 37 attempts,
29 successes, 7 rejected paragraphs, 2 deadline skips and 1 timeout. Fallbacks kept sessions
running. These counts describe model reliability, not its effect on scores. The batch used the
`louis/subagent-team` base with the candidate safeguards; it is diagnostic evidence only.

Observations from the arena and the data package, with evidence. An entry says what happened and
how often, not what to do; what the agent does is in `design.md`. Most entries rest on one to
three sessions with one supplier. The sandbox bots are deterministic per sheet path; the practice
suppliers vary 1 to 2 % between runs with the same sheets. Sessions: `exports/` (schema in
`exports/README.md`), `logs/sessions/`, `logs/runs/`. Tags: `arena` seen in a session, `data` from
the package, `rules` from `docs/api.md` or the kit.

## Hidden-case readiness (Sunday 09:15 to 10:00)

content.thinking: Found strong headline numbers: 10/10 practice cases closed at 0.777 mean, #3 of 24 teams, and top scores on P05/P18, plus an €1.17M savings claim I'll verify from the session data before using it. Now I'll use these to propose sections for the writeup.

questions.question: Top of page: which of these do you want?

options.label: Hero banner
options.description: Custom SVG banner: ProcureCabana wordmark, tagline, EHL Grand Finale Munich 2026 · Tacto track. Renders in GitHub light and dark.

options.label: Mask hook
options.description: Open with the slide-1 story: €4.50 a mask, 5.7 bn bought, €2.3 bn still in court. 'Nobody negotiated that price. ProcureCabana would have.'

options.label: Numbers strip
options.description: Four big figures in a row: 10/10 deals · 0.777 mean score · #3 of 24 teams · €1.17M saved (after I recompute it).

options.label: Demo visual
options.description: Keep the pipeline monitor screenshot, or I record a short GIF of the P05 replay so the page moves.

questions.question: Results: which do you want?

options.label: Beat the record
options.description: Callout: on P05 and P18 we beat the best score of all 24 teams; on P11 0.710 vs the house agent's 0.314.

options.label: Scorecard
options.description: Per-case table: our score, best of all teams, Tacto house agent. Ten rows, no jargon.

options.label: Live Final
options.description: A results section for the Live Final, left empty now and filled once the waves are scored after 12:00.

options.label: Euros per case
options.description: Opening quote vs our deal in euros for each case, so the savings are concrete, not just a score.

questions.question: Story: which do you want?

options.label: One deal replayed
options.description: P05 as a short story: the supplier, our anchor, their counters, the close at 27.86 on our second sheet.

options.label: How it works, 3 lines
options.description: Prepare, Negotiate, Close & learn, one plain sentence each, plus the system map image. No file names.

#!/bin/zsh
# Live Final launcher: at START (HHMM, default 1145) it freezes origin/main in its own worktree,
# runs the tests (falls back to the verified FALLBACK commit if they fail), records the hash and
# starts the final runner. DRY=1 stops the runner after 60 s (a rehearsal of the 403 wait).
REPO=/Users/stef/Projects/ehlcodacabana-final
RUN=/Users/stef/Projects/ehl-final-run
START=${START:-1145}
FALLBACK=d78759e
LOG=$REPO/logs/final-launch.status
say() { echo "$(date +%T) $*" >> $LOG; }

until [[ $(date +%H%M) -ge $START ]]; do sleep 10; done
say "launch (dry=${DRY:-0})"
cd $REPO
for i in 1 2 3; do git fetch -q origin && break; say "fetch failed ($i)"; sleep 5; done
git worktree remove --force $RUN 2>/dev/null
git worktree add -q --detach $RUN origin/main || { say "worktree on origin/main failed, using $FALLBACK"; git worktree add -q --detach $RUN $FALLBACK; }
cd $RUN
ln -sf $REPO/.env .env
ln -sfn $REPO/data data
rm -rf logs && ln -sfn $REPO/logs logs
uv sync -q >> $LOG 2>&1
if uv run pytest -q -x > $REPO/logs/final-pytest.log 2>&1; then
  say "tests pass on $(git rev-parse --short HEAD)"
else
  say "tests FAILED on $(git rev-parse --short HEAD), switching to $FALLBACK"
  git checkout -q --detach $FALLBACK && uv sync -q >> $LOG 2>&1
fi
git rev-parse HEAD > $REPO/logs/final.hash
say "runner start on $(git rev-parse --short HEAD) (hash in logs/final.hash)"
if [[ -n $DRY ]]; then
  uv run buyer run --set final --parallel 10 -v > $REPO/logs/final-dry.log 2>&1 &
  F=$!; sleep 60
  if kill -0 $F 2>/dev/null; then say "dry: runner alive after 60s, stopping"; kill -INT $F; sleep 3; kill $F 2>/dev/null
  else wait $F; say "dry: runner EXITED early: $?"; fi
else
  uv run buyer run --set final --parallel 10 -v > $REPO/logs/final.log 2>&1
  say "runner exited: $?"
fi
say "done"

"""Hero banner and numbers strip for the README, as self-contained SVG."""

import math
import sys
from pathlib import Path

OUT = Path(sys.argv[1])
INK, INK2 = "#0F1724", "#1A2638"
ORANGE, SAND, MUTED, WHITE = "#F26B3A", "#F5D9B8", "#93A1B5", "#FFFFFF"
FONT = "Inter, -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif"


def waves(w, h, n=18, amp=26, period=220, phase_step=0.0, stroke=11):
    """Copacabana promenade: parallel sine bands."""
    out = []
    for i in range(n):
        y0 = -40 + i * (h + 80) / n
        pts = []
        for x in range(-20, w + 21, 8):
            y = y0 + amp * math.sin(2 * math.pi * x / period + i * phase_step)
            pts.append(f"{x},{y:.1f}")
        out.append(f'<polyline points="{" ".join(pts)}" />')
    return (
        f'<g fill="none" stroke="{WHITE}" stroke-width="{stroke}" stroke-linecap="round">'
        + "".join(out)
        + "</g>"
    )


def banner():
    w, h = 1280, 420
    prices = [138.55, 134.10, 132.20, 131.10, 129.90, 129.70]
    # price ladder card
    cx, cy, cw, ch = 820, 78, 400, 264
    px0, px1 = cx + 40, cx + cw - 40
    py0, py1 = cy + 92, cy + ch - 58
    hi, lo = max(prices), min(prices)

    def pt(i, p):
        x = px0 + i * (px1 - px0) / (len(prices) - 1)
        y = py0 + (hi - p) / (hi - lo) * (py1 - py0)
        return x, y

    pts = [pt(i, p) for i, p in enumerate(prices)]
    line = " ".join(f"{x:.1f},{y:.1f}" for x, y in pts)
    area = f"{pts[0][0]:.1f},{py1 + 8} " + line + f" {pts[-1][0]:.1f},{py1 + 8}"
    dots = "".join(
        f'<circle cx="{x:.1f}" cy="{y:.1f}" r="4.5" fill="{INK}" stroke="{SAND}" stroke-width="2"/>'
        for x, y in pts[:-1]
    )
    ex, ey = pts[-1]
    sx, sy = pts[0]
    return f"""<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="{w}" height="{h}" viewBox="0 0 {w} {h}" role="img" aria-label="ProcureCabana: the AI buyer that negotiates by e-mail and closes the cheapest deal on its own">
  <defs>
    <linearGradient id="bg" x1="0" y1="0" x2="1" y2="1">
      <stop offset="0" stop-color="{INK}"/><stop offset="1" stop-color="{INK2}"/>
    </linearGradient>
    <linearGradient id="fade" x1="0" y1="0" x2="1" y2="0">
      <stop offset="0.25" stop-color="#fff" stop-opacity="0"/><stop offset="1" stop-color="#fff" stop-opacity="1"/>
    </linearGradient>
    <mask id="m"><rect width="{w}" height="{h}" fill="url(#fade)"/></mask>
    <linearGradient id="area" x1="0" y1="0" x2="0" y2="1">
      <stop offset="0" stop-color="{ORANGE}" stop-opacity="0.35"/><stop offset="1" stop-color="{ORANGE}" stop-opacity="0"/>
    </linearGradient>
    <clipPath id="c"><rect width="{w}" height="{h}" rx="22"/></clipPath>
  </defs>
  <g clip-path="url(#c)">
    <rect width="{w}" height="{h}" fill="url(#bg)"/>
    <g mask="url(#m)" opacity="0.07">{waves(w, h)}</g>
    <rect x="0" y="{h - 6}" width="{w}" height="6" fill="{ORANGE}"/>
  </g>
  <g font-family="{FONT}">

> **€4.50 a mask. From anyone. In any quantity.** > > In 2020 Germany's Federal Ministry of Health promised to buy every FFP2 mask offered to it, at > one fixed price. It bought 5.7 billion masks for €5.9 billion. About 2 billion were ever handed > out; most of the rest was destroyed. €2.3 billion is still in court, with a ruling due on > 15 December 2026. > > **Nobody negotiated that price. ProcureCabana would have.** > > Sources: Tagesspiegel, ZDF, Handelsblatt (September 2026); Bund der Steuerzahler.

![One negotiation replayed: the agents at work on the left, the e-mail thread with the supplier on the right](docs/assets/pipeline-monitor.webp)

One negotiation replayed: the agents at work on the left, the e-mail thread with the supplier on the right.

## How it works 1. **Prepare.** Before the first e-mail, a team of AI researchers studies the supplier's history, documents and costs, then rehearses the negotiation against a simulated supplier. 2. **Negotiate.** For every reply, an analyst reads the supplier's mood and tactic, code sets the price and terms, and a writer turns them into an e-mail that cites hard evidence. 3. **Close and learn.** Code accepts the cheapest valid offer across all suppliers, or walks away, and the outcome is remembered for the next similar case. ## Scorecard Share of the best possible saving each negotiation captured. 100 % is the cheapest deal the supplier would ever have agreed to. | Negotiation | ProcureCabana | Best of 24 teams | Tacto's own agent | |---|---:|---:|---:| | A foundry announces +9.5 % on pump casings | **99.9 %** | 99.5 % | 96.6 % | | A motor maker passes on rising copper prices | **73.5 %** | 84.7 % | 74.0 % | | Renewing the frame agreement for a frequency converter | **93.3 %** | 93.6 % | 92.5 % | | Renewing the ball bearing agreement | **86.0 %** | 87.4 % | 86.0 % | | Tender for the shaft of a new pump series | **82.8 %** | 82.4 % | 55.5 % | | Bundling the fastener kit with one distributor | **76.0 %** | 77.9 % | 78.2 % | | Alloy surcharge on stainless steel bar, distributor A | **74.8 %** | 91.6 % | 75.2 % | | Alloy surcharge on stainless steel bar, distributor B | **75.6 %** | 67.7 % | 38.6 % | | A seal supplier cuts our allocation | **71.0 %** | 70.2 % | 68.6 % | | Bearing brackets from a supplier with a red quality score | **79.4 %** | 80.7 % | 31.4 % | | **Average** | **81.2 %** | 83.6 % | 69.7 % | ProcureCabana: our best negotiation per case on the hosted practice set, as of Sunday 11 October. Best of 24 teams and Tacto's own agent: the practice board on Saturday night. The numbers above the screenshot come from a single run through all ten cases. ## Read more - [The paper](writeup/writeup.pdf): our approach in two pages - [The pitch deck](docs/slides/EHL_Codacabana_Slide_Deck.pdf) ## The challenge ProcureCabana was built at the European Hackathon League Grand Finale in Munich, 10 to 11 October 2026, for the challenge set by [Tacto](https://www.tacto.ai). Our agent buys for Hollerau Pumpenwerke, a fictional pump maker, and negotiates with Tacto's supplier bots. A deal is judged on its total cost over the contract, not on the unit price alone: payment terms, delivery, contract length, quality and index clauses all count. ## Team Codacabana - Steffen Grabert ([@stegra05](https://github.com/stegra05)) - Louis Heinrich ([@louis-heinrich](https://github.com/louis-heinrich)) - Julian Fritz ([@jfr77](https://github.com/jfr77)) - João Zuffo ([@Zuff2004](https://github.com/Zuff2004))

# Codacabana: Tacto Negotiation Arena

An AI buyer that negotiates by e-mail with supplier bots and closes the deal with the lowest
total cost, or walks away.

Built by Team Codacabana at the European Hackathon League Grand Finale, Munich, 10 to 11 October
2026, on the Tacto track. The buyer works for Hollerau Pumpenwerke, a fictional pump maker. Each
case is scored on how much of the possible saving it captures:
`(C_open - C_deal) / (C_open - C_best)`. Brief: [docs/challenge.md](docs/challenge.md).

![Pipeline monitor replaying a test run: prepare, negotiate, close and learn, with the live supplier thread beside it](docs/assets/pipeline-monitor.webp)

*The pipeline monitor in [`pitch/`](pitch/README.md) replaying a simulated case, with the live
supplier thread on the right.*

## How it works

**Code owns every binding number; the model owns words.** Prices, term sheets, accepts and
walk-aways are computed and checked with the arena's exact cost function (`total_cost`,
`must_haves_ok`). Models read, argue and write, but cannot change a figure.

| Stage | What happens | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **Prepare** | Four specialist researchers (economics, persona, history, leverage) and a lead build one supplier brief. A supplier and a buyer subagent then rehearse the arguments into a playbook. | [`research.py`](buyer/research.py), [`rehearsal.py`](buyer/rehearsal.py) |
| **Negotiate** | For each supplier reply: the live analyst reads the mood and tactic, the decision engine sets price and terms, the writer turns them into an e-mail with claims cited by data ID. | [`analyst.py`](buyer/analyst.py), [`policy.py`](buyer/policy.py), [`economics.py`](buyer/economics.py), [`claims.py`](buyer/claims.py), [`writer.py`](buyer/writer.py) |
| **Close & learn** | The close gate accepts the cheapest valid standing sheet across suppliers, or walks. A debrief saves the outcome for the next similar case. | [`policy.py`](buyer/policy.py), [`memory.py`](buyer/memory.py) |

The [runner](buyer/runner.py) orchestrates each case: it answers the oldest reply first and
keeps every move inside the arena's 60 second clock, whatever fails. The agent branches on what
the data says about a supplier, never on a case or supplier ID.

Read more:

- [writeup/writeup.pdf](writeup/writeup.pdf): the two-page paper on the approach, with the system diagram
- [docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md): the module map of the running system
- [docs/design.md](docs/design.md): what the agent does and why
- [docs/learnings.md](docs/learnings.md): what practice showed, with evidence

## Quick start

Python 3.12 and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/).

```sh
git config core.hooksPath .githooks   # secret scan, no pushes to main, Entire hooks
uv sync                               # the agent, Tacto's arena kit, pytest, ruff
cp .env.example .env                  # fill in the keys below
uv run arena data                     # data package into data/package
uv run arena me                       # the key works: team and practice quota
```

| Variable | What |
|---|---|
| `ARENA_URL` | `https://arena.tacto.ai` |
| `ARENA_API_KEY` | the team key from https://arena.tacto.ai/apply |
| `ARENA_DATA` | `data/package` |
| `LLM_BASE_URL`, `LLM_MODEL`, `LLM_API_KEY` | the model, any OpenAI-compatible chat completions endpoint; optional `LLM_EFFORT` |

## Run

```sh
uv run buyer play case:D01 -v                     # one sandbox case (free)
uv run buyer run --set practice --parallel 10     # every hosted practice case (counts against the quota)
uv run buyer pull --set practice                  # finished sessions with trace -> logs/sessions/
uv run buyer run --set final --parallel 10 -v     # the Live Final: start before 12:00, leave it running
```

## Pipeline monitor

The screenshot above is a small web app that replays one recorded case step by step: which
component acted, what it decided, and the e-mails that went back and forth.

```sh
cd pitch && npm install && npm run dev
```

It plays a bundled trace from the local simulator, so it needs no API key. Details in
[pitch/README.md](pitch/README.md).

## Develop

Rules for people and coding agents: [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md).

```sh
uv run pytest -q                 # our agent end to end against the local arena simulator
uv run ruff check . && uv run ruff format --check .
```

## Repo map

| Path | What |
|---|---|
| `buyer/` | the agent |
| `tests/` | end-to-end tests against `arena-sim` |
| `pitch/` | the pipeline monitor |
| `docs/` | brief, API, design, architecture, learnings, submission checklist |
| `writeup/` | the paper (`tectonic writeup/writeup.tex` builds it) |
| `analysis/`, `exports/`, `logs/` | exploration, Saturday's sessions as CSV, traces |
